title: Wine-List Design and Inventory Management
quiz.0.question: When designing a distinctive Italian list, besides the three pillars (Piemonte/Toscana/Veneto), what do sommeliers usually add to show professionalism?
quiz.0.options.1: Offering only the cheapest table wines (Vino da Tavola)
quiz.0.options.2: Adding lesser-known but high-quality areas or grapes, such as Sicily's Etna Rosso or Campania's Fiano
quiz.0.options.3: Tripling the price of every wine
quiz.0.explanation: A great list must balance "classics" and "exploration". Adding emerging or lesser-known areas such as Etna or native white grapes shows the list's depth and the sommelier's eye, attracting advanced enthusiasts.
quiz.1.question: Which pricing strategy do modern restaurants most often use to encourage guests to buy higher-priced wines while securing margins on entry-level wines?
quiz.1.options.0: A flat markup: every wine multiplied by 3
quiz.1.options.1: A sliding scale: the lower the cost, the higher the multiplier; the higher the cost, the lower the multiplier
quiz.1.options.2: One uniform price for every wine
quiz.1.explanation: A sliding scale stops expensive wines becoming sky-high under a fixed multiplier (and therefore unsellable), while the lower multiplier encourages guests to "trade up", earning more absolute cash profit.
quiz.2.question: What is the industry's most common "golden rule" for pricing wine by the glass (BTG)?
quiz.2.options.0: The price of one glass should equal the purchase cost of the whole bottle
quiz.2.options.1: The price of one glass should be half the bottle's list price
quiz.2.options.2: Wine by the glass should be free to attract guests
quiz.2.options.3: A glass should cost far more than buying the whole bottle
quiz.2.explanation: To control the risk of waste (an opened bottle not selling out and oxidising), the industry standard is to price the first glass at the bottle's purchase cost. Selling the first glass recovers the cost, and the rest is pure profit.
quiz.3.question: A restaurant wants to offer a top aged Barolo by the glass on its BTG list. What is the most effective way to avoid oxidation after opening?
quiz.3.options.2: Using a system such as Coravin that injects inert gas (argon) without removing the cork
quiz.3.options.3: Making guests buy two glasses at once
quiz.3.explanation: The Coravin system draws wine through a fine needle that pierces the cork, while argon fills the space left behind to keep oxygen out. When the needle is removed the cork reseals naturally, so the remaining wine can keep for months or even years — an essential tool for serving expensive wines by the glass.
slides.0.title: Wine-List Design and Inventory Management
slides.0.subtitle: From selection to profit: building an Italian wine list with both taste and commercial value
slides.1.title: Three Core Principles of Wine-List Design
slides.1.content:
A great wine list is more than a list of names — it is an extension of the restaurant's soul and a key tool for creating profit. When designing a list you must balance "expertise", "guests' needs" and "commercial return".

Principle one

Fit with the menu

The list must be tightly linked to the restaurant's cooking style (a northern Italian restaurant, a seafood restaurant and a pizzeria each have different needs); offer enough pairing choices that every dish has a fitting wine; a list without a sense of pairing is a failed list

Principle two

Balance of style and price

Cover every style from fresh to rich; offer a full price range from entry-level wines to icon wines; satisfy both the guest choosing an everyday wine and the collector seeking a treasured bottle

Principle three

Readability and navigation

Avoid overly technical jargon (DOCG/DOC/IGT mean nothing to ordinary guests); you can organise by "flavour style" (crisp whites/full reds/sweet wines); the goal is for guests to find the wine they want within 3 minutes
slides.2.title: Building a Distinctive Italian List: Three Pillars + Surprises to Explore
slides.2.content:
Italy has 350+ native grapes and 20 regions. A list with depth must strike the perfect balance between "essential classics" and "surprises to explore".

⭐ The three pillars (the indispensable foundation)

  • Piemonte: Barolo + Barbaresco (Nebbiolo), everyday Barbera d'Asti
  • Toscana: Chianti Classico + Brunello di Montalcino (Sangiovese), Super Tuscans
  • Veneto: Amarone della Valpolicella, Prosecco, Soave
  • These three areas are the cornerstone for attracting traditional consumers — no Italian list can do without them

🔍 Surprises to explore (showing professional depth)

  • The rising South: Sicily's Etna Rosso (Nerello Mascalese), Campania's Taurasi (Aglianico)
  • The white-grape revival: Sardinia's Vermentino, the Marche's Verdicchio, Campania's Fiano di Avellino
  • Orange and natural wines: Friuli's skin-contact whites, appealing to modern consumers who value sustainability and character
  • Shows the sommelier's eye and depth, bringing advanced enthusiasts back
slides.3.title: Pricing Strategy: A Sliding Scale Instead of a Flat Markup
slides.3.content:
Restaurant wine pricing directly affects margins and sales speed. The traditional "flat markup" has given way to the modern "sliding scale", the key to raising overall revenue.

❌ Traditional: Flat Markup

  • Every purchase price multiplied by a fixed factor (usually 3x)
  • ⚠️ Cheap wines (cost $10 → sell $30): too little profit to cover staff and service costs
  • ⚠️ Expensive wines (cost $100 → sell $300): sky-high prices nobody pays, tying up capital in stock
  • Result: neither enough profit nor encouragement for guests to trade up

✅ Modern: Sliding Scale

  • Principle: the lower the cost, the higher the multiplier; the higher the cost, the lower the multiplier
  • Entry-level wines: cost $10 × 3.5 → sell $35 (securing a basic margin)
  • Mid-range wines: cost $30 × 2.5 → sell $75
  • Top wines: cost $100 × 1.5 → sell $150 (encouraging trading up and earning more cash profit)
slides.4.title: The BTG Golden Rule, Inventory Management and Coravin
slides.4.content:
🥂 The BTG golden rule

"The first glass must recover the bottle's purchase cost"

For a bottle costing $15 (pouring 5-6 glasses), price the first glass at $15; selling the first glass recovers the cost and the rest is pure profit; a BTG list should include: sparkling ×1, white ×2, red ×2, sweet ×1

📊 Managing stock turnover

Regularly checking for dead stock

Review sales data regularly through the POS system; slow sellers can be moved through active staff recommendations, pairing menus or themed dinners; don't leave capital tied up in wine that won't sell

🔬 The Coravin preservation system

Letting top old wines be served safely by the glass

A fine needle pierces the cork to draw the wine while argon fills the space; after the needle is removed the cork reseals naturally; the remaining wine can keep for months without oxidising; it makes a $50+ glass of aged Barolo possible

🎓 Themed tasting events

Vertical vs horizontal tastings

Vertical: several vintages from one estate, showing the effect of vintage and ageing potential; horizontal: different estates from the same area and vintage, showing different interpretations of terroir — the most effective framework for wine education, and an elegant way to move stock
slides.5.title: Key Takeaways
slides.5.points.0: Three core principles of list design: fit with the menu, balance of style and price, readability and navigation — none can be missing
slides.5.points.1: The three pillars of an Italian list: Piemonte (Barolo/Barbaresco), Toscana (Chianti/Brunello), Veneto (Amarone/Prosecco)
slides.5.points.2: Elements to explore: lesser-known gems such as Etna Rosso, Taurasi and Fiano show the sommelier's depth and attract advanced enthusiasts
slides.5.points.3: The drawback of a traditional flat markup: expensive wines become unsellable, cheap wines earn too little — a lose-lose at both ends
slides.5.points.4: The modern sliding scale: high multipliers for low-cost wines, low multipliers for high-cost wines — making expensive wines better value and cheap wines profitable
slides.5.points.5: The BTG golden rule: the first glass is priced at the bottle's purchase cost — selling the first glass recovers the cost, and the rest is pure profit
slides.5.points.6: Inventory management: regularly use the POS system to find dead stock and move it through pairing menus or themed dinners
slides.5.points.7: The Coravin system: drawing wine with argon without removing the cork, letting top old wines be served safely by the glass without oxidising for months
